decks.title: Lines and Angles: Part 1, angles, linear pairs and vertically opposite angles
goals: Describe rays, line segments, lines and angles
Classify angles as acute, right, obtuse, straight, reflex or complete
Prove the linear pair theorem and that vertically opposite angles are equal
Use angle facts at a point to find unknown angles

slides.heading: Angles are everywhere
slides.body_md: An **angle** is the amount of turn between two rays that start at the same point. Look at the hands of a clock or a half-open door.

visual.alt: Two rays OA and OB starting from the same point O. They are the arms of an angle AOB, which measures 50 degrees. The point O is the vertex.
visual.caption: Angle $AOB$ has vertex $O$ and arms $OA$ and $OB$.

slides.narration: Look at the corner of a book, the hands of a clock or a half-open classroom door. Each one shows an angle. An angle is formed when two rays start from the same point, and its size tells us how far one ray has turned away from the other. In this chapter we study angles, pairs of angles and the lines that make them.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Name **rays**, **segments** and **lines**, and **angles**
Classify angles by size
Prove the **linear pair theorem** and the **vertically opposite angles theorem**
Use **angles at a point** to find unknown angles

visual.alt: Flow of Part 1: rays and angles, types of angle, the linear pair theorem and its proof, and vertically opposite angles and their proof.
visual.caption: Part 1 road map.

slides.narration: In this part we start with rays and angles and the names for different sizes of angle. Then we prove two important theorems: angles in a linear pair add up to one hundred eighty degrees, and vertically opposite angles are equal. We finish by using these facts to find unknown angles.

slides.heading: Line, segment and ray
slides.body_md: A **line segment** $AB$ has two end points. A **line** $CD$ goes on for ever in both directions. A **ray** $PE$ starts at $P$ and goes on for ever through $E$.

visual.alt: Three drawings. A segment AB with two end points. A line CD that goes on in both directions. A ray PE that starts at P and goes on beyond E.
visual.caption: A segment has two ends, a line has none, and a ray has one starting point.

slides.narration: A line segment has two end points and a fixed length. A line has no end points, and it goes on for ever in both directions. A ray has one starting point and goes on for ever in one direction. Rays are the building blocks of angles, because every angle is made from two rays with the same starting point.

slides.heading: What is an angle?
slides.body_md: Two rays $OA$ and $OB$ with the same starting point $O$ form an angle. $O$ is the **vertex**, and $OA$ and $OB$ are the **arms**. We write $\angle AOB = 50^\circ$ and measure it in **degrees**.

visual.alt: Two rays OA and OB starting from the same point O. They are the arms of an angle AOB, which measures 50 degrees. The point O is the vertex.
visual.caption: Angle $AOB$ has vertex $O$ and arms $OA$ and $OB$.

slides.narration: Two rays that start at the same point form an angle. The common point is the vertex, and the two rays are the arms of the angle. In the figure the rays are O A and O B, and the angle measures fifty degrees. We measure angles in degrees, where a full turn all the way round is three hundred sixty degrees.

slides.heading: Types of angle
slides.body_md: We name an angle by comparing it with $90^\circ$, $180^\circ$ and $360^\circ$.

visual.alt: Table of angle types: acute between 0 and 90 degrees, for example 35; right exactly 90; obtuse between 90 and 180, for example 125; straight exactly 180; reflex between 180 and 360, for example 250; complete exactly 360.
visual.caption: Classify an angle by comparing it with $90^\circ$, $180^\circ$ and $360^\circ$.

slides.narration: Angles have names that depend on their size. An acute angle is smaller than a right angle. A right angle is exactly ninety degrees. An obtuse angle is bigger than ninety but smaller than one hundred eighty. A straight angle is exactly one hundred eighty. A reflex angle is bigger than one hundred eighty, and a complete angle is a full turn of three hundred sixty degrees.

slides.heading: Quick check: name the angle
slides.body_md: An angle measures two hundred fifteen degrees. What kind of angle is it?

visual.alt: Three angles side by side: an acute angle of 40 degrees, a right angle of 90 degrees marked with a square corner, and an obtuse angle of 130 degrees.
visual.caption: Acute $40^\circ$, right $90^\circ$, obtuse $130^\circ$.

slides.narration: Compare the angle with one hundred eighty and three hundred sixty.

slides.heading: Complementary and supplementary angles
slides.body_md: Two angles are **complementary** if they add up to $90^\circ$, and **supplementary** if they add up to $180^\circ$. Here $35^\circ + 55^\circ = 90^\circ$ and $110^\circ + 70^\circ = 180^\circ$.

visual.alt: Left: a right angle split into 35 degrees and 55 degrees, which are complementary. Right: a straight line with a ray, making 110 degrees and 70 degrees, which are supplementary.
visual.caption: Complementary: $35^\circ + 55^\circ = 90^\circ$. Supplementary: $110^\circ + 70^\circ = 180^\circ$.

slides.narration: Two angles are complementary if they add up to ninety degrees, and supplementary if they add up to one hundred eighty degrees. On the left, thirty-five and fifty-five make a right angle. On the right, one hundred ten and seventy make a straight angle. The complement of an angle x is ninety minus x, and its supplement is one hundred eighty minus x.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: complement and supplement
slides.body_md: Find the angle in each case.
bullets: **$20^\circ$ more than its complement —** $x = (90 - x) + 20$ gives $2x = 110$, so $x = 55^\circ$
**Supplement is $4$ times the complement —** $180 - x = 4(90 - x)$ gives $3x = 180$, so $x = 60^\circ$

rows: An angle is $20^\circ$ more than its complement
The supplement of an angle is $4$ times its complement

visual.alt: Table of two conditions on an angle x. If x is 20 degrees more than its complement, then x equals 90 minus x plus 20, so x is 55 degrees. If its supplement is 4 times its complement, then 180 minus x equals 4 times 90 minus x, so x is 60 degrees.
visual.caption: Write the condition as an equation in $x$.

slides.narration: In the first case, write the angle as x. Its complement is ninety minus x, and the angle is twenty more than that. Solving gives fifty-five degrees. In the second case, the supplement one hundred eighty minus x equals four times the complement. Solving gives sixty degrees. Always check by substituting back.

slides.heading: Linear pair
slides.body_md: When a ray $OC$ stands on a line $AB$, the two angles $\angle AOC$ and $\angle COB$ next to each other form a **linear pair**.

visual.alt: A straight line AB with a point O on it and a ray OC standing on the line. The two angles AOC and COB next to each other are called x and y. Together they make a straight angle.
visual.caption: A linear pair: $\angle AOC = x$ and $\angle COB = y$ with $x + y = 180^\circ$.

slides.narration: When a ray stands on a straight line, it makes two angles next to each other. They share an arm, and their other arms form the straight line. Such a pair of angles is called a linear pair. The linear pair theorem says that the two angles always add up to one hundred eighty degrees. Now we prove it.

slides.heading: Proof of the linear pair theorem
slides.body_md: **Theorem:** If a ray stands on a line, the sum of the two adjacent angles is $180^\circ$. The proof uses a perpendicular $OD$ and the idea that a whole angle is the sum of its parts.

visual.alt: Table: the linear pair theorem is proved in four steps. Draw OD at right angles to AB; add 90 and the angle DOC to get AOC; subtract the angle DOC from 90 to get COB; adding gives 180 degrees. With 25 and 65 degrees in the figure, 115 plus 65 is 180.
visual.caption: The angles of a linear pair always add up to $180^\circ$.

slides.narration: Draw O D at right angles to the line A B. Then the angle A O C is ninety degrees plus the angle D O C. The angle C O B is ninety degrees minus the angle D O C, because O C lies inside the right angle D O B. Add the two. The angle D O C cancels, and the sum is ninety plus ninety, which is one hundred eighty degrees.

slides.heading: Quick check: a linear pair
slides.body_md: Two angles of a linear pair are in the ratio two to seven. What is the larger angle?

visual.alt: A straight line AB with a point O on it and a ray OC standing on the line. The two angles AOC and COB next to each other are called x and y. Together they make a straight angle.
visual.caption: A linear pair: $\angle AOC = x$ and $\angle COB = y$ with $x + y = 180^\circ$.

slides.narration: The two angles add up to one hundred eighty degrees. Divide it in the ratio.

slides.heading: Vertically opposite angles
slides.body_md: When two lines cross, the angles that face each other are **vertically opposite angles**. In the figure, $\angle BOC$ and $\angle AOD$ are a pair, and $\angle COA$ and $\angle DOB$ are another pair.

visual.alt: Two straight lines AB and CD crossing at O. The opposite angles BOC and AOD are both 65 degrees, and the other two opposite angles COA and DOB are both 115 degrees.
visual.caption: Vertically opposite angles are equal: $65^\circ = 65^\circ$ and $115^\circ = 115^\circ$.

slides.narration: When two straight lines cross, they make four angles. The angles that face each other, across the crossing point, are called vertically opposite angles. In the figure the two angles of sixty-five degrees are opposite each other, and so are the two angles of one hundred fifteen degrees. Vertically opposite angles always seem to be equal. Let us prove it.

slides.heading: Vertically opposite angles are equal
slides.body_md: **Theorem:** If two lines intersect, the vertically opposite angles are equal. Each of the two angles makes a linear pair with the same angle, $\angle COB$.

rows: Linear pair: ray $OC$ stands on line $AB$
Linear pair: ray $OB$ stands on line $CD$
Both equal $180^\circ$ (things equal to the same thing)
Take $\angle COB$ from both sides (equals taken from equals)
Similarly, using the linear pairs at $O$ on the other side

visual.alt: Table: vertically opposite angles are equal. Angle AOC plus angle COB is 180 and angle COB plus angle BOD is 180, so the two sums are equal. Taking away the angle COB from both sides gives angle AOC equal to angle BOD. In the same way angle COB equals angle AOD.
visual.caption: Each vertically opposite angle makes a linear pair with the same adjacent angle.

slides.narration: Each of the two angles, A O C and B O D, makes a linear pair with the same angle C O B. So both A O C plus C O B and C O B plus B O D are one hundred eighty degrees. These two sums are equal, so taking away the angle C O B from both sides leaves the angle A O C equal to the angle B O D.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: find x
slides.body_md: Lines $AB$ and $CD$ cross at $O$, with $\angle AOC = (2x + 15)^\circ$ and $\angle BOD = (3x - 10)^\circ$. Find $x$, $\angle AOC$ and $\angle BOC$.
bullets: **Equal angles —** vertically opposite: $2x + 15 = 3x - 10$, so $x = 25$
**$\angle AOC$ —** $2 \times 25 + 15 = 65^\circ$
**$\angle BOC$ —** linear pair: $180^\circ - 65^\circ = 115^\circ$

visual.alt: Two lines AB and CD crossing at O. The angle AOC is marked 2x plus 15 degrees and its vertically opposite angle BOD is marked 3x minus 10 degrees. The angle BOC is marked with a question mark.
visual.caption: $\angle AOC = (2x + 15)^\circ$ and $\angle BOD = (3x - 10)^\circ$.

slides.narration: The angles A O C and B O D are vertically opposite, so they are equal. Setting two x plus fifteen equal to three x minus ten gives x equal to twenty-five. Then the angle A O C is sixty-five degrees. The angle B O C makes a linear pair with it, so it is one hundred eighty minus sixty-five, which is one hundred fifteen degrees.

slides.heading: Quick check: vertically opposite
slides.body_md: Two lines cross and one angle is seventy-two degrees. What is the angle next to it, on a straight line?

visual.alt: Two straight lines AB and CD crossing at O. The opposite angles BOC and AOD are both 65 degrees, and the other two opposite angles COA and DOB are both 115 degrees.
visual.caption: Vertically opposite angles are equal: $65^\circ = 65^\circ$ and $115^\circ = 115^\circ$.

slides.narration: Angles on a straight line add up to one hundred eighty degrees.

slides.heading: Angles around a point
slides.body_md: Rays from one point $O$ divide a full turn into angles that add up to $360^\circ$. Here $70^\circ + 95^\circ + 110^\circ + 85^\circ = 360^\circ$.

visual.alt: Four rays from a point O making angles of 70, 95, 110 and 85 degrees one after the other. Together they go all the way round the point.
visual.caption: Angles around a point: $70^\circ + 95^\circ + 110^\circ + 85^\circ = 360^\circ$.

slides.narration: If several rays start from the same point, the angles between them fill a full turn. So the angles around a point always add up to three hundred sixty degrees. In the figure, seventy, ninety-five, one hundred ten and eighty-five degrees make three hundred sixty in total. A straight line is the special case of two rays pointing in opposite directions, with one hundred eighty degrees on each side.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: around a point
slides.body_md: Four angles around a point are $x$, $2x$, $(x + 60)^\circ$ and $100^\circ$. Find $x$ and all four angles.
bullets: **Angles —** $50^\circ$, $100^\circ$, $110^\circ$, $100^\circ$, which total $360^\circ$

visual.alt: Table of the four angles around a point: 50, 100, 110 and 100 degrees, which total 360 degrees.
visual.caption: The angles around a point add up to $360^\circ$.

slides.narration: Angles around a point add up to three hundred sixty degrees. So x plus two x plus x plus sixty plus one hundred equals three hundred sixty. Collecting terms gives four x plus one hundred sixty equals three hundred sixty, so x is fifty. The four angles are fifty, one hundred, one hundred ten and one hundred degrees, and they do add up to three hundred sixty.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: An angle is formed by **two rays** with a common vertex; types: acute, right, obtuse, straight, reflex, complete
Complementary angles add to $90^\circ$; supplementary angles add to $180^\circ$
**Linear pair theorem:** the angles of a linear pair add up to $180^\circ$
**Vertically opposite angles** are equal
Angles around a point add up to $360^\circ$

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 1: angles of a linear pair add up to 180 degrees, vertically opposite angles are equal, and angles around a point add up to 360 degrees.
visual.caption: Three facts about angles at a point.

slides.narration: To sum up. An angle is made by two rays with a common vertex. Complementary angles add to ninety degrees and supplementary angles add to one hundred eighty. The angles of a linear pair add up to one hundred eighty degrees, and vertically opposite angles are equal. Angles around a point add up to three hundred sixty degrees.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Finding angles (1–2 marks):** write the equation, solve, then state each angle
**Proofs (3 marks):** every step needs a reason in brackets
**Always name the fact:** linear pair, vertically opposite, angles at a point
**Mistake:** treating any two adjacent angles as a linear pair
**Mistake:** solving for $x$ and forgetting to find the angle
slides.narration: In angle questions, write an equation, solve it, and then state each angle that was asked for. In proofs, write a reason beside every step. Name the fact you use, such as linear pair or vertically opposite angles. Two common slips: calling any two adjacent angles a linear pair, and finding x but forgetting to find the angle.

decks.title: Lines and Angles: Part 2, parallel lines, transversals and proof by contradiction
goals: Name the pairs of angles made by a transversal
Use the angle rules and their converses for parallel lines
Explain why lines parallel to the same line are parallel to each other
Follow and write simple proofs by contradiction

slides.heading: Parallel lines and a transversal
slides.body_md: Railway lines never meet, and a crossing track cuts them at the same angle. A line that cuts two or more lines is called a **transversal**.

visual.alt: Two parallel lines l and m, marked with arrows, cut by a transversal t. The angle between t and l on the upper right is 65 degrees, and the matching angle at m is also 65 degrees.
visual.caption: Parallel lines cut by a transversal: matching angles are equal.

slides.narration: Think of two railway tracks running side by side, and a footpath that crosses both. The tracks are parallel, which means they never meet. The crossing path is a transversal, a line that cuts two or more lines. It makes the same angle with both tracks, and in this part we see what that tells us.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Name **corresponding**, **alternate interior** and **co-interior** angles
Use the **angle rules** when lines are parallel and their **converses** as tests
Show that lines parallel to the **same line** are parallel
Follow **proofs by contradiction**

visual.alt: Flow of Part 2: the eight angles and their names, the angle rules for parallel lines, the converse tests, parallel lines to the same line, and proof by contradiction.
visual.caption: Part 2 road map.

slides.narration: First we name the eight angles made by a transversal, and learn the rules for parallel lines. Then we use the converses of those rules to show that two lines are parallel. We see why lines parallel to the same line are parallel to each other, and we study a new way of proving things, called proof by contradiction.

slides.heading: The eight angles
slides.body_md: A transversal $t$ cuts two lines $l$ and $m$ and makes **eight angles**. We number them $1$ to $4$ at the upper crossing and $5$ to $8$ at the lower crossing.

visual.alt: Two parallel lines l and m cut by a transversal t. The eight angles are numbered 1 to 4 at the upper crossing and 5 to 8 at the lower crossing, going round from the upper left.
visual.caption: The eight angles. Angles $1$ and $5$ are corresponding; $3$ and $5$ are alternate interior; $3$ and $6$ are co-interior.

slides.narration: A transversal cuts two lines and makes eight angles. We number them one to four at the upper crossing, and five to eight at the lower crossing, going round in the same order. The four angles between the two lines are called interior angles, and the other four are exterior angles. Next we name some special pairs.

slides.heading: Corresponding, alternate and co-interior
slides.body_md: **Corresponding:** same position at each crossing. **Alternate interior:** between the lines and on opposite sides of $t$. **Co-interior:** between the lines and on the same side of $t$.

visual.alt: Table of angle pairs for parallel lines cut by a transversal. Corresponding angles such as 1 and 5 are equal, both 115 degrees. Alternate interior angles such as 3 and 5 are equal. Co-interior angles such as 3 and 6 are 115 and 65 degrees and add up to 180 degrees.
visual.caption: Three kinds of angle pair made by a transversal.

slides.narration: Corresponding angles are in the same position at the two crossings, like angle one and angle five. Alternate interior angles are between the lines and on opposite sides of the transversal, like three and five. Co-interior angles are between the lines and on the same side, like three and six. For parallel lines, the first two kinds are equal, and co-interior angles add up to one hundred eighty.

slides.heading: The corresponding angles axiom
slides.body_md: **Axiom:** if a transversal cuts two **parallel** lines, each pair of corresponding angles is equal. In the figure $\angle 1 = \angle 5 = 115^\circ$.

visual.alt: Parallel lines l and m with a transversal t. The upper left angle at l and the upper left angle at m are corresponding angles, and both are 115 degrees.
visual.caption: Corresponding angles ($\angle 1$ and $\angle 5$) are equal when $l \parallel m$.

slides.narration: The corresponding angles axiom says that if a transversal cuts two parallel lines, then each pair of corresponding angles is equal. In the figure the upper left angle at the first line and the upper left angle at the second line are both one hundred fifteen degrees. We accept this without proof, and prove the other angle rules from it.

slides.heading: Alternate and co-interior angles
slides.body_md: From the corresponding angles axiom, with the help of vertically opposite angles and linear pairs, we prove that **alternate interior angles are equal** and **co-interior angles add up to $180^\circ$**.

rows: Both equal $\angle 1$: alternate interior angles are equal
Replace $\angle 2$ by $\angle 6$: co-interior angles add up to $180^\circ$

visual.alt: Table of two proofs for parallel lines l and m. Angle 3 equals angle 1 because they are vertically opposite, and angle 1 equals angle 5 by the corresponding angles axiom, so angle 3 equals angle 5. Then angle 2 plus angle 3 is 180 by the linear pair, and angle 2 equals angle 6, so angle 6 plus angle 3 is 180.
visual.caption: Alternate interior angles are equal and co-interior angles are supplementary.

slides.narration: Angle three equals angle one, because they are vertically opposite. Angle one equals angle five by the corresponding angles axiom. So angle three equals angle five, which shows that alternate interior angles are equal. For co-interior angles, angle two plus angle three is one hundred eighty by the linear pair, and angle two equals angle six. So angle six plus angle three is one hundred eighty.

slides.heading: Quick check: pairs of angles
slides.body_md: In the figure, which pair of angles is a pair of alternate interior angles?

visual.alt: Two parallel lines l and m cut by a transversal t. The eight angles are numbered 1 to 4 at the upper crossing and 5 to 8 at the lower crossing, going round from the upper left.
visual.caption: The eight angles. Angles $1$ and $5$ are corresponding; $3$ and $5$ are alternate interior; $3$ and $6$ are co-interior.

slides.narration: Alternate interior angles lie between the lines and on opposite sides of the transversal.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: find all eight angles
slides.body_md: In the figure $l \parallel m$ and $\angle 2 = 65^\circ$. Find the other seven angles, with reasons.
bullets: **$\angle 1$ —** linear pair with $\angle 2$: $180^\circ - 65^\circ = 115^\circ$
**$\angle 3$ and $\angle 4$ —** vertically opposite: $115^\circ$ and $65^\circ$
**$\angle 5$ to $\angle 8$ —** corresponding to $\angle 1$ to $\angle 4$: $115^\circ$, $65^\circ$, $115^\circ$, $65^\circ$

visual.alt: Parallel lines l and m cut by a transversal t with all eight angles marked: at each crossing the angles are 115, 65, 115 and 65 degrees going round.
visual.caption: If one angle is $65^\circ$, the other seven are $65^\circ$ or $115^\circ$.

slides.narration: We know angle two is sixty-five degrees. Angle one forms a linear pair with it, so it is one hundred fifteen. Angle three is vertically opposite angle one, and angle four is vertically opposite angle two. The four angles at the lower crossing are corresponding to those, so they have the same values. In all, four angles are sixty-five and four are one hundred fifteen degrees.

slides.heading: The converse: tests for parallel lines
slides.body_md: If a transversal makes **equal corresponding angles**, **equal alternate interior angles** or **co-interior angles adding up to $180^\circ$**, the two lines are parallel. In the figure the alternate angles $\angle 3 = \angle 5 = 110^\circ$, so $l \parallel m$.

visual.alt: Two lines l and m cut by a transversal t so that the alternate interior angles 3 and 5 are both 110 degrees. This shows that the lines l and m are parallel.
visual.caption: Equal alternate interior angles ($110^\circ$ each) tell us that $l \parallel m$.

slides.narration: The rules also work the other way round. If a transversal makes equal corresponding angles, or equal alternate interior angles, or co-interior angles that add up to one hundred eighty degrees, then the two lines must be parallel. In the figure the alternate interior angles are both one hundred ten degrees, so the lines are parallel. This is how we test that two lines are parallel.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: find x
slides.body_md: The lines $l$ and $m$ are parallel. (a) Alternate interior angles are $(2x + 10)^\circ$ and $(3x - 20)^\circ$. (b) Co-interior angles are $(x + 20)^\circ$ and $(2x + 10)^\circ$. Find $x$ in each case.
bullets: **(a)** equal: $2x + 10 = 3x - 20$, so $x = 30$ and each angle is $70^\circ$
**(b)** sum $180^\circ$: $3x + 30 = 180$, so $x = 50$ and the angles are $70^\circ$ and $110^\circ$

rows: Alternate interior angles $(2x + 10)^\circ$ and $(3x - 20)^\circ$, with $l \parallel m$

visual.alt: Table: for alternate interior angles 2x plus 10 and 3x minus 20, set them equal to get x equal to 30 and both angles 70 degrees. For co-interior angles x plus 20 and 2x plus 10, set the sum equal to 180 to get x equal to 50 and angles 70 and 110 degrees.
visual.caption: Choose the rule that matches the pair of angles.

slides.narration: Choose the rule that matches the pair of angles. Alternate interior angles are equal, so two x plus ten equals three x minus twenty, and x is thirty. Each angle is seventy degrees. Co-interior angles add up to one hundred eighty, so three x plus thirty equals one hundred eighty, and x is fifty. The angles are seventy and one hundred ten degrees.

slides.heading: Quick check: co-interior angles
slides.body_md: The lines are parallel, and one co-interior angle is seventy-four degrees. What is the other?

visual.alt: Parallel lines l and m with a transversal t. The two angles between the lines on the same side of t are 115 degrees and 65 degrees, which add up to 180 degrees.
visual.caption: Co-interior angles: $115^\circ + 65^\circ = 180^\circ$.

slides.narration: Co-interior angles add up to one hundred eighty degrees.

slides.heading: Lines parallel to the same line
slides.body_md: **Theorem:** if $l \parallel m$ and $m \parallel n$, then $l \parallel n$. A transversal makes $65^\circ$ with $l$; by corresponding angles it also makes $65^\circ$ with $m$, and then with $n$. So the corresponding angles of $l$ and $n$ are equal, and $l \parallel n$.

visual.alt: Three parallel lines l, m and n, each marked with an arrow, cut by one transversal t. At every crossing the angle on the upper right is 65 degrees, so the corresponding angles are all equal.
visual.caption: If $l \parallel m$ and $m \parallel n$, a transversal makes the same angle with all three, so $l \parallel n$.

slides.narration: Suppose line l is parallel to line m, and line m is parallel to line n. Draw a transversal. It makes sixty-five degrees with l, so it makes sixty-five degrees with m, because l and m are parallel. And since m is parallel to n, it makes sixty-five degrees with n as well. Then the corresponding angles for l and n are equal, so l is parallel to n.

slides.heading: A result proved from parallel lines: the angle sum of a triangle
slides.body_md: This result belongs to the next chapter on triangles, but parallel lines prove it at once. Through $A$ draw $PQ \parallel BC$. Then $\angle PAB = \angle B$ and $\angle QAC = \angle C$, and the three angles at $A$ make a straight angle. So the angles of a triangle add up to $180^\circ$.

visual.alt: A triangle ABC with angles of 50 degrees at B and 60 degrees at C. A line PQ through A is drawn parallel to BC. The alternate angles PAB and CAQ are 50 and 60 degrees, and the three angles at A, 50, 70 and 60, make a straight angle of 180 degrees.
visual.caption: $PQ \parallel BC$ gives $\angle PAB = \angle B$ and $\angle QAC = \angle C$, so $\angle A + \angle B + \angle C = 180^\circ$.

slides.narration: Here is a result that we prove from parallel lines. Take any triangle and draw a line through one corner parallel to the opposite side. The alternate angles at that corner equal the two other angles of the triangle. Together with the angle of the triangle, they make a straight angle. So the three angles of any triangle add up to one hundred eighty degrees.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a bent path
slides.body_md: $l \parallel m$. A path goes from $A$ on $l$ to $E$ between the lines and then to $C$ on $m$. The angle at $A$ with $l$ is $35^\circ$ and the angle at $C$ with $m$ is $40^\circ$. Find $\angle AEC$.
bullets: **Draw a helper —** a line through $E$ parallel to $l$ and $m$
**Alternate angles —** one part of $\angle AEC$ is $35^\circ$ and the other part is $40^\circ$
**Add —** $\angle AEC = 35^\circ + 40^\circ = 75^\circ$

visual.alt: Two \parallel lines l and m. A bent path runs from A on l to a point E between the lines and on to C on m. The angle at A between l and AE is 35 degrees and the angle at C between m and CE is 40 degrees. A dashed line through E is parallel to both lines. The angle AEC is marked with a question mark.
visual.caption: $l \parallel m$. The dashed line through $E$ is parallel to both, so $\angle AEC = 35^\circ + 40^\circ$.

slides.narration: Draw a helper line through E parallel to both lines. The angle at A between the line l and the path is equal to the part of the angle at E on the same side, because they are alternate angles. The same holds at C. So the angle at E is thirty-five plus forty, which is seventy-five degrees. Drawing a helper parallel line is a very useful idea.

slides.heading: Proof by contradiction
slides.body_md: To prove a statement by **contradiction**, assume that it is **false**, reason carefully, and reach something that cannot be true. Then the statement must be true.

nodes.label: Assume the opposite of what is to be proved
So the original statement is true

visual.alt: Flow chart of proof by contradiction: assume the opposite of the claim, reason correctly, reach a contradiction with a known fact, and conclude that the claim is true.
visual.caption: The steps of a proof by contradiction.

slides.narration: There is another way to prove a statement. Assume that the statement is false. Then reason carefully from that assumption. If you reach a result that cannot be true, such as something that contradicts a known fact, the assumption must have been wrong. So the original statement is true. This method is called proof by contradiction.

**(b)** If $n$ were odd, $n = 2k + 1$ and $n^2 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1$ would be odd, a contradiction

slides.heading: Two lines meet in at most one point
slides.body_md: Two different lines cannot meet in two points. **Assume** they meet at $P$ and $Q$. Then two different lines pass through $P$ and $Q$, but only **one** line passes through two given points. This **contradicts** Euclid's first postulate, so the lines meet in at most one point.

But we know that exactly one line passes through two given points. This is a contradiction, so our supposition was wrong. Two different lines meet in at most one point.

sections.heading: 1. Rays, lines and angles
sections.body_md: A **line segment** has two end points, a **line** has none, and a **ray** has one starting point. Two rays with a common starting point form an **angle**; the point is the **vertex** and the rays are the **arms**. Angles are measured in degrees; a full turn is $360^\circ$.

key_terms.definition_md: The figure formed by two rays with a common starting point, the vertex.
A part of a line that starts at a point and goes on for ever in one direction.

sections.heading: 2. Types of angle
sections.body_md:
Acute: less than $90^\circ$. Right: $90^\circ$. Obtuse: between $90^\circ$ and $180^\circ$. Straight: $180^\circ$. Reflex: between $180^\circ$ and $360^\circ$. Complete: $360^\circ$.

Two angles are **complementary** if they add up to $90^\circ$ and **supplementary** if they add up to $180^\circ$. The complement of $x$ is $90 - x$ and its supplement is $180 - x$.

key_terms.definition_md: Two angles that add up to $90^\circ$.
Two angles that add up to $180^\circ$.

sections.heading: 3. Linear pair
sections.body_md:
When a ray stands on a line, the two adjacent angles form a **linear pair**.

**Theorem:** the angles of a linear pair add up to $180^\circ$.

*Proof idea:* draw $OD \perp AB$. Then $\angle AOC = 90^\circ + \angle DOC$ and $\angle COB = 90^\circ - \angle DOC$, and the sum is $180^\circ$. The **converse** is also true: if two adjacent angles add up to $180^\circ$, their outer arms form a straight line.

key_terms.definition_md: Two adjacent angles whose outer arms form a straight line.

visual.alt: A straight line AB with a point O on it and a ray OC standing on the line. The two angles AOC and COB next to each other are called x and y. Together they make a straight angle.
visual.caption: A linear pair: $\angle AOC = x$ and $\angle COB = y$ with $x + y = 180^\circ$.

visuals.alt: A straight line AB with the ray OD at right angles to it, and a ray OC between OD and OB. The angle DOC is 25 degrees and the angle COB is 65 degrees, so the angle AOC is 90 plus 25, which is 115 degrees.
visuals.caption: Proof figure: $OD \perp AB$. Here $\angle DOC = 25^\circ$ and $\angle COB = 65^\circ$.

visuals.alt: Table: the linear pair theorem is proved in four steps. Draw OD at right angles to AB; add 90 and the angle DOC to get AOC; subtract the angle DOC from 90 to get COB; adding gives 180 degrees. With 25 and 65 degrees in the figure, 115 plus 65 is 180.
visuals.caption: The angles of a linear pair always add up to $180^\circ$.

sections.heading: 4. Vertically opposite angles
sections.body_md:
When two lines cross, the angles that face each other are **vertically opposite angles**.

**Theorem:** vertically opposite angles are equal.

*Proof:* $\angle AOC + \angle COB = 180^\circ = \angle COB + \angle BOD$, so $\angle AOC = \angle BOD$.

Angles around a point add up to $360^\circ$.

key_terms.definition_md: The angles that face each other when two lines cross.

visual.caption: Vertically opposite angles are equal: $65^\circ = 65^\circ$ and $115^\circ = 115^\circ$.

Similarly, using the linear pairs at $O$ on the other side

sections.heading: 5. Parallel lines and a transversal
sections.body_md:
A **transversal** cuts two or more lines. It makes **corresponding**, **alternate interior** and **co-interior** angles.

**Corresponding angles axiom:** if $l \parallel m$, corresponding angles are equal. From it: alternate interior angles are equal and co-interior angles add up to $180^\circ$.

**Converse:** if corresponding angles are equal, or alternate interior angles are equal, or co-interior angles add up to $180^\circ$, then $l \parallel m$.

**Transitivity:** lines parallel to the same line are parallel to each other.

A result proved from parallel lines: through a vertex of a triangle draw a line parallel to the opposite side; this shows that the angles of a triangle add up to $180^\circ$ (triangles are studied in the next chapter).

key_terms.definition_md: A line that cuts two or more lines.
Interior angles on the same side of the transversal.

sections.heading: 6. Proof by contradiction
sections.body_md:
To prove a statement by **contradiction**: (1) assume that it is false; (2) reason correctly from the assumption; (3) reach a result that contradicts a known fact; (4) conclude that the statement is true.

Examples: there is no largest even number ($N + 2$ would be larger); if $n^2$ is even then $n$ is even (if $n = 2k + 1$ then $n^2$ is odd); two different lines meet in at most one point (otherwise two lines would pass through two points).

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Finding angles (1–2 marks):* write the equation, solve it, state the angle.
- *Proofs (3 marks):* every step with a reason in brackets.
- *Parallel lines (2–3 marks):* name the pair of angles and the rule or test used.
- *Contradiction (3 marks):* assumption, reasoning, contradiction, conclusion.

**Common mistakes**
1. Calling any two adjacent angles a linear pair.
2. Using angle rules for lines that are not known to be parallel.
3. Confusing alternate interior with co-interior angles.
4. Finding $x$ but not the angle asked for.
5. Forgetting the concluding sentence in a proof by contradiction.

questions.stem_md: An angle measures $215^\circ$. It is
questions.solution_md: An angle between $180^\circ$ and $360^\circ$ is a reflex angle, and $215^\circ$ lies between them. An obtuse angle is less than $180^\circ$, a straight angle is exactly $180^\circ$, and an acute angle is less than $90^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: Two angles of a linear pair are in the ratio $2 : 7$. The larger angle is
questions.solution_md: The angles of a linear pair add up to $180^\circ$, and $2 + 7 = 9$ parts, so one part is $180 \div 9 = 20^\circ$. The larger angle is $7 \times 20 = 140^\circ$ (the smaller is $40^\circ$). The value $126^\circ$ comes from dividing by $10$ parts.

questions.stem_md: Two straight lines $AB$ and $CD$ cross at $O$ and $\angle BOC = 72^\circ$. Then $\angle COA$ is
questions.solution_md: $\angle BOC$ and $\angle COA$ form a linear pair on the line $AB$, so $\angle COA = 180^\circ - 72^\circ = 108^\circ$. The angle $72^\circ$ is $\angle AOD$, which is vertically opposite $\angle BOC$.

questions.solution_md: Alternate interior angles lie between the two lines on opposite sides of the transversal: $\angle 3$ and $\angle 5$. The pair $\angle 1$ and $\angle 5$ is a corresponding pair, $\angle 3$ and $\angle 6$ are co-interior, and $\angle 1$ and $\angle 3$ are vertically opposite.

options.text_md: assume that there is a largest even number
assume that there is no largest even number

questions.solution_md: A proof by contradiction starts by assuming the opposite of what we want to prove. We want to prove that there is no largest even number, so we assume that there is one, and then look for a contradiction.

questions.stem_md: The complement of $38^\circ$ is
questions.solution_md: Complementary angles add up to $90^\circ$, so the complement is $90^\circ - 38^\circ = 52^\circ$. The value $142^\circ$ is the supplement.

questions.stem_md: The supplement of an angle is three times its complement. The angle is
questions.solution_md: Let the angle be $x$. Then $180 - x = 3(90 - x)$, so $180 - x = 270 - 3x$ and $2x = 90$, so $x = 45^\circ$. Check: the supplement is $135^\circ$ and the complement is $45^\circ$, and $3 \times 45 = 135$.

questions.stem_md: Four roads meet at a junction in Ludhiana, and the angles between them, going round the junction, are $x^\circ$, $2x^\circ$, $3x^\circ$ and $120^\circ$. The value of $x$ is
questions.solution_md: Angles around a point add up to $360^\circ$, so $x + 2x + 3x + 120 = 360$, that is $6x = 240$ and $x = 40$. The angles are $40^\circ$, $80^\circ$, $120^\circ$ and $120^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: Lines $AB$ and $CD$ cross at $O$, with $\angle AOC = (3x + 5)^\circ$ and $\angle BOD = (5x - 35)^\circ$. Then $\angle AOC$ is
questions.solution_md: The angles are vertically opposite, so $3x + 5 = 5x - 35$, giving $x = 20$. Then $\angle AOC = 3 \times 20 + 5 = 65^\circ$. The value $115^\circ$ is the adjacent angle and $20^\circ$ is $x$ itself.

questions.stem_md: A ray $OC$ stands on a line $AB$ at $O$, and $\angle AOC = 3 \times \angle COB$. Then $\angle COB$ is
questions.solution_md: Let $\angle COB = y$. The angles form a linear pair, so $3y + y = 180$, giving $y = 45^\circ$. Then $\angle AOC = 135^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: When two straight lines cross, the number of pairs of vertically opposite angles is
questions.solution_md: Two crossing lines make four angles. Each angle has exactly one angle opposite it, so the four angles form $2$ pairs of vertically opposite angles.

questions.stem_md: A pair of interior angles on the same side of a transversal that cuts two parallel lines are in the ratio $4 : 5$. The smaller of the two angles is
questions.solution_md: Co-interior angles between parallel lines add up to $180^\circ$, and $4 + 5 = 9$ parts, so one part is $20^\circ$. The smaller angle is $4 \times 20 = 80^\circ$ and the larger is $100^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: Lines $l$, $m$ and $n$ are such that $l \parallel m$ and $m \parallel n$. A transversal makes an angle of $125^\circ$ with $l$. The corresponding angle that it makes with $n$ is
questions.solution_md: The transversal makes $125^\circ$ with $l$, so by the corresponding angles axiom it makes $125^\circ$ with $m$, since $l \parallel m$. Then, since $m \parallel n$, it makes $125^\circ$ with $n$. In other words $l \parallel n$ and the corresponding angles are equal. The value $55^\circ$ is the adjacent angle.

questions.stem_md: The lines $l$ and $m$ are parallel and a transversal makes alternate interior angles $(4x - 20)^\circ$ and $(2x + 30)^\circ$. The value of $x$ is

questions.stem_md: (a) Write the four steps of a proof by contradiction. (b) Prove by contradiction that if $n^2$ is even, then $n$ is even. (c) Show that $n = 14$ and $n = 15$ agree with this result. (d) Prove by contradiction that there is no largest even number. (e) A triangle has angles that add up to $180^\circ$ (proved from parallel lines in this chapter). Prove by contradiction that a triangle cannot have two right angles.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Assume the statement is false; reason correctly from the assumption; reach a result that contradicts a known fact; conclude that the statement is true.

**(b)** Suppose $n^2$ is even but $n$ is odd, $n = 2k + 1$. Then $n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1$, which is odd. This contradicts $n^2$ being even, so $n$ is even.

**(c)** $14^2 = 196$ is even and $14$ is even. $15^2 = 225$ is odd and $15$ is odd.

**(d)** Suppose $N$ is the largest even number. Then $N + 2$ is even and greater than $N$, a contradiction.

**(e)** Suppose a triangle has two right angles. Then the sum of two angles is $90^\circ + 90^\circ = 180^\circ$, so the third angle would be $180^\circ - 180^\circ = 0^\circ$, which is impossible. So a triangle cannot have two right angles.

children.solution_md: The roads cross at $O$, and $\angle AOC$ and $\angle BOD$ face each other across $O$, so they are vertically opposite and therefore equal. A linear pair would share an arm, and complementary angles add up to $90^\circ$.
Vertically opposite angles are equal: $3x + 10 = 5x - 30$, so $2x = 40$ and $x = 20$.

answer.model_answer_md: $\angle AOC = 3 \times 20 + 10 = 70^\circ$. $\angle AOD$ and $\angle AOC$ form a linear pair on the line $CD$, so $\angle AOD = 180^\circ - 70^\circ = 110^\circ$.

questions.passage_md: Two parallel rails $l$ and $m$ of a railway track near Chennai are crossed by a footpath $t$. In the figure, $\angle 2 = 65^\circ$.

children.solution_md: $\angle 6$ and $\angle 2$ are corresponding angles between the parallel rails, so $\angle 6 = \angle 2 = 65^\circ$. The value $115^\circ$ is $\angle 3$.
$\angle 2$ and $\angle 3$ form a linear pair on the line $t$, so $\angle 3 = 180^\circ - 65^\circ = 115^\circ$.

children.stem_md: **(i)** Find $\angle 5$ and name the type of angle pair that $\angle 3$ and $\angle 5$ form.

answer.model_answer_md: $\angle 3$ and $\angle 5$ are alternate interior angles between parallel lines, so $\angle 5 = \angle 3 = 180^\circ - 65^\circ = 115^\circ$ (as $\angle 2 = 65^\circ$).

alternatives.stem_md: **(ii)** A third rail $n$ is parallel to $m$. What angle does the footpath make with $n$ in the same position as $\angle 2$? Give the reason.

answer.model_answer_md: Since $l \parallel m$ and $m \parallel n$, the rails $l$ and $n$ are parallel (lines parallel to the same line are parallel). So the corresponding angle at $n$ is also $65^\circ$.

alternatives.solution_md: Transitivity of parallel lines, then corresponding angles.

questions.passage_md: Ravi says: "There is a largest even number, $N$." His classmate Ayesha wants to show that he is wrong, using a proof by contradiction.

children.stem_md: Which fact does Ayesha use to contradict Ravi?

options.text_md: $N - 2$ is an even number smaller than $N$
$N + 2$ is an even number bigger than $N$

children.solution_md: Adding $2$ to an even number gives another even number, and it is bigger. So $N$ cannot be the largest even number. The numbers $N - 2$ and $2N$ do not give a bigger even number.

children.stem_md: Ravi says that $N = 1000000$ is the largest even number. Find an even number that is greater than it, by Ayesha's method.
children.solution_md: $N + 2 = 1000000 + 2 = 1000002$, which is even and greater than $N$.

children.stem_md: **(i)** Write Ayesha's proof in three lines: assumption, reasoning, conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Assume** that $N$ is the largest even number.

**Reason:** $N + 2$ is also even and $N + 2 > N$, which contradicts the choice of $N$.

**Conclude:** the assumption is false, so there is no largest even number.

alternatives.stem_md: **(ii)** Use a similar proof to show that there is no greatest odd number.

answer.model_answer_md: Suppose $M$ is the greatest odd number. Then $M + 2$ is also odd and $M + 2 > M$, which contradicts the choice of $M$. So there is no greatest odd number.

alternatives.solution_md: Add 2 to the supposed greatest odd number.
